notes.meaning: God answers Moses' fear of speaking by giving him authority like God's own before Pharaoh. Moses would act with divine power to direct the mission, while his brother Aaron would serve as his spokesman to deliver the words.

God laid out a clear line of communication for His servants. Moses was to pass on everything God commanded to Aaron, and Aaron was to speak directly to Pharaoh with the unchanging demand to set Israel free.

The Lord told Moses in advance that Pharaoh would resist, even while God performed many miracles across the land. God used Pharaoh's resistance to show His supreme power and authority over the ruler of Egypt.

differ.view: God sovereignly ordained the hardening of Pharaoh's heart before the plagues began so that His power and righteous justice would be displayed.
God did not cause Pharaoh to sin, but withdrew His restraining grace and allowed Pharaoh's own rebellious choices to harden his heart.

notes.meaning: Pharaoh would stubbornly ignore the divine message. In response, God promised to strike Egypt with mighty acts of judgment and bring His people out in orderly ranks like an army.

The ultimate goal of the plagues was to show the Egyptians that the God of Israel is the one true Lord. When He used His power to rescue the Israelites, all Egypt would see that their own gods were powerless.
Moses and Aaron set aside their earlier doubts and did exactly what the Lord commanded. Their hesitation ended as they moved forward in steady obedience.

Moses was eighty years old and Aaron was eighty-three when they stood before Pharaoh. Their advanced age showed that this rescue relied on God's sustaining power rather than human youth or natural strength.

God prepared His messengers for their meeting by telling them that Pharaoh would ask for proof of their authority. When the king demanded a sign, Aaron was to throw down his staff, and God would turn it into a serpent.
Moses and Aaron entered the royal court and followed God's instructions completely. Aaron cast his staff down in front of Pharaoh and his royal officials, and it instantly became a serpent.
Pharaoh called on his own wise men, sorcerers, and court magicians to challenge the sign. Using their secret arts, they managed to produce a similar result.
Each magician threw down his staff, and they also appeared as serpents. Aaron's staff then swallowed up all their staffs, proving that God's power easily overcomes any rival power.
Even after seeing his magicians defeated, Pharaoh remained stubborn and closed his mind to the truth. He refused to listen to God's messengers, exactly as the Lord had said.
God pointed out that Pharaoh's heart had become completely stiff and unyielding. The king stubbornly refused to let the people go, so God prepared to strike Egypt with painful judgments.

God told Moses to confront Pharaoh the next morning at the bank of the Nile River, holding the staff that had turned into a snake. Moses was to remind the king that the God of the Hebrews demanded Israel's release to worship Him in the wilderness, but Pharaoh had refused to obey.
Moses warned Pharaoh that he would soon experience the Lord's power firsthand. Aaron would strike the water of the Nile with his staff, and the entire river would turn into blood.
This blow would destroy Egypt's primary source of life. The fish would die, the river would rot and smell foul, and the Egyptians would be unable to drink the water they depended on.

God commanded Aaron to stretch his staff over all the waters of Egypt, including canals, pools, reservoirs, and household jars of wood and stone. This showed that every single water supply in the nation was under God's control.
Moses and Aaron obeyed the Lord in plain sight of Pharaoh and his court. Aaron raised his staff and struck the Nile, and all the water across the river turned to blood right before their eyes.
The fish died, the river smelled terrible, and nobody could drink from it. This disaster ruined their food supply and proved that the river the Egyptians worshipped could not save itself from God.
The Egyptian magicians used their arts to make a small amount of water look like blood. Seeing this small imitation gave Pharaoh an excuse to keep his heart hard and ignore God's messengers.

Pharaoh turned his back on the scene and walked into his palace without caring about what had happened. He refused to think seriously about God's warning, showing cold neglect for his people's suffering.
The ordinary Egyptian people were forced to dig into the ground along the riverbanks to find drinkable water. The river they had always relied on was ruined, leaving them desperate for relief.
The plague of blood lasted for seven full days before God brought it to an end. This gave Pharaoh plenty of time to rethink his pride, yet he still refused to turn to the Lord.
